_about: Languages and software used for economic models, for /translate-code and tools/translate.py. kind: statistical, numerical, model, optimization, bayesian, legacy, spreadsheet, database. source: the studio reads and translates from it. target: the studio translates to it. toolchain: the name in studio-config.yaml toolchains.approved that covers it (null if none). run: how a program is run in batch. pitfalls: semantics that most often change results when code moves to another language.

languages.name: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, linearmodels)
pitfalls: Indexing starts at 0 and slices exclude the end point (x[0:3] is three elements).
NumPy std and var default to ddof=0 (population); pandas std and var default to ddof=1.
round() and numpy.round round half to even (2.5 becomes 2); Stata, MATLAB, SAS and Excel round half away from zero.
pandas aligns on the index when assigning a Series, so rows can be silently reordered or set to NaN.
NumPy arrays are row-major by default; reshape from MATLAB, Fortran, R or Julia needs order='F'.
Comparisons with NaN are False, so filters drop missing values silently.
pandas sort_values is not stable for a single key unless kind='mergesort' or 'stable'.
statsmodels OLS has no constant unless the formula interface or add_constant is used.

languages.name: R
pitfalls: NA propagates: mean(x) is NA unless na.rm = TRUE; lm() drops incomplete rows by default (na.action).
round() rounds half to even (round(2.5) is 2).
sandwich::vcovHC defaults to HC3; Stata's robust errors are HC1.
quantile() defaults to type 7; Stata and SAS use other definitions.
Factors: the base level is the first level (alphabetical unless set), which changes dummy coefficients.
Vectors recycle silently when lengths differ.
dplyr::lag shifts by position and ignores gaps in the time index; use a panel-aware lag.
Before R 4.0, data.frame() and read.csv() turned strings into factors by default.
Results can depend on package versions; pin them with renv.

languages.name: Stata (do-files, ado-files, Mata)
languages.tests: assert statements in a test do-file
pitfalls: Missing values (., .a to .z) are larger than any number, so 'if x > 5' includes missing values.
generate creates float (about 7 significant digits) unless the type is given or set type double is used.
Time-series operators (L., D., F.) respect gaps in the time variable; positional shifts in other languages do not.
sort is not stable unless the stable option is used; results that depend on order within ties change between runs.
vce(robust) is HC1; vce(cluster) applies the small-sample factor G/(G-1)*(N-1)/(N-K).
xtreg, fe reports a constant (the average of the fixed effects) and its own degrees of freedom; areg differs.
Commands depend on the version statement and on user-written packages (ssc), which change over time.
_pctile and summarize, detail use the empirical distribution with averaging (R type 2); altdef gives another definition.
Local and global macros are expanded before execution; a misspelled macro expands to an empty string without error.
Daily dates count days since 1 January 1960.

languages.name: MATLAB (with Econometrics, Optimization and Statistics toolboxes)
pitfalls: Indexing starts at 1 and arrays are column-major.
A\b solves least squares when A is not square; numpy.linalg.solve fails instead.
' is the conjugate transpose; .' is the plain transpose (they differ for complex matrices).
Scripts share the base workspace and global variables; hidden state can carry between runs.
quantile uses the midpoint definition (R type 5); prctile likewise.
Toolbox functions change outputs across releases (for example the outputs of hpfilter).
Implicit expansion (R2016b and later) broadcasts silently where older code would have failed.
round rounds half away from zero.
Dates as datenum count days since year 0.

languages.name: GNU Octave
pitfalls: Mostly MATLAB-compatible, but toolbox functions live in packages (statistics, optim) with different defaults.
Accepts syntax MATLAB rejects (#comments, endif, ++, printf), so Octave code may not run in MATLAB.
Some MATLAB functions are missing or behave differently (tables, datetime, string arrays).

languages.name: Julia
pitfalls: Indexing starts at 1 and arrays are column-major.
Integer overflow wraps silently (typemax(Int) + 1 is negative).
Broadcasting needs the dot (x .+ y, f.(x)); missing dots change the meaning or fail.
missing propagates and is different from NaN and nothing.
The random-number stream for a given seed can change between Julia versions; pin the version and use StableRNGs where draws must reproduce.
Integer division is div or ÷; / always returns a float.

languages.name: Dynare (.mod files, run in MATLAB or Octave)
languages.tests: steady-state residuals and IRF regression tests
pitfalls: Timing: a stock variable carries the date of the period in which it is chosen, so capital in production is k(-1).
Variables are in levels unless the model is written in logs or model(linear) is used; IRFs are then deviations in levels.
steady_state_model computes the steady state analytically; steady with initval solves it numerically and can find another solution.
stoch_simul options (order, pruning, periods, irf, hp_filter) change the moments and IRFs reported.
Theoretical moments and simulated moments (periods > 0) differ.
Prior shapes in estimated_params are parameterized by mean and standard deviation, not by the distribution's own parameters.
The macro processor (@#define, @#if, @#for) generates the model text; translate the expanded model, not the macro code.
Shock blocks set either the standard deviation (stderr) or the variance (var).

languages.name: IRIS toolbox (MATLAB; .model files)
pitfalls: Model files declare !transition_variables, !measurement_variables, !log_variables; log variables change what deviations mean.
Lags are written x{-1}; steady-state references use &x.
Simulation and filtering options (anticipate, deviation, method) change results.
Databases (struct of Series) carry their own date ranges; ranges must match in the target.

languages.name: RISE toolbox (MATLAB; regime-switching models)
pitfalls: Regime-switching solutions depend on the solution concept and the transition matrix specification.
Few other tools solve Markov-switching DSGE models; check that the target supports the solution concept before translating.

languages.name: EViews (programs and workfiles)
pitfalls: The sample (smpl) is state that persists across commands and programs until changed.
Every estimation writes its coefficients to the default vector c, which later equations may read.
Equations need an explicit constant (c) in ls.
Model objects solve with options (dynamic or static, Gauss-Seidel or Newton, add factors) that change the solution.
Frequency conversion defaults differ by series and setting (average, sum, last).
Program variables: !name are numbers, %name are strings, and arguments are %0, %1, ...
Built-in filters choose defaults by frequency (for example the HP lambda).

languages.name: SAS (data step, PROCs, macro language)
pitfalls: The data step loops implicitly over rows through the program data vector; RETAIN keeps values across rows.
LAG() is a queue: inside a conditional it returns the value from the last time that statement ran, not the previous row.
Missing numeric values are smaller than any number.
MERGE with BY does not form a Cartesian product for many-to-many matches, unlike SQL joins.
FIRST. and LAST. BY-group flags need the data sorted by the BY variables.
PROC LOGISTIC models the probability of the lowest response value unless DESCENDING or EVENT= is given.
Formats change how values print and group, not the stored values.
The macro language (%let, &var, %macro) generates code before it runs.
Dates count days since 1 January 1960.

languages.name: SPSS syntax
pitfalls: Transformations are pending until a procedure or EXECUTE runs.
User-missing values (declared codes such as 99) differ from system-missing values; both must be carried over.
LAG works on the cases that pass the current filter.
SPLIT FILE and WEIGHT change every later procedure until turned off.

languages.name: GAUSS
pitfalls: Indexing starts at 1; .* and ./ are element-wise, * is matrix multiplication, ' is transpose.
Procedures return values with retp and can read and change global variables.
Missing values are a special NaN-like code handled by miss() and packr(); behavior depends on settings.
Many published econometric codes (1990s and 2000s) rely on library procedures that must be found and translated too.

languages.name: RATS / WinRATS
pitfalls: CALENDAR and ALLOCATE set the date frame for all later instructions.
Entry ranges on instructions (start end) silently restrict the sample.
Procedures (@name) are separate source files that must be included in the translation.

languages.name: gretl (hansl scripts)
pitfalls: The sample (smpl) is state that persists across commands.
Robust standard errors depend on settings (set hc_version).

languages.name: Ox
pitfalls: Indexing starts at 0, unlike GAUSS and MATLAB from which Ox code is often ported.
Packages (PcGive, SsfPack, G@RCH) carry their own estimators and defaults.

languages.name: LIMDEP / NLOGIT
pitfalls: Commands use their own syntax ($ terminators, ; separators) and estimator defaults that must be checked against the manual.

languages.name: TSP
pitfalls: SMPL state persists; FREQ and date conventions set the frame for every later command.

languages.name: TROLL (macroeconometric models)
pitfalls: Model equations, add factors and exogenized paths live in separate files and archives.
Simulation algorithm and convergence settings (Newton, stacked time) change results.
Large macroeconometric models depend on databanks with their own frequencies and missing codes.

languages.name: FAME / AREMOS (time-series databases and scripts)
pitfalls: Several missing-value codes (NA, NC, ND) carry different meanings.
Frequency conversion and observed attributes (averaged, summed, end of period) are properties of each series.
Translation usually means re-implementing the data pipeline, not the models.

languages.name: GAMS (CGE and optimization models)
languages.tests: benchmark replication (zero-shock) and model status checks
pitfalls: Variables are free unless declared positive; bounds (.lo, .up) and fixings (.fx) define the closure.
Dollar conditions ($) restrict equations and sums to subsets; dropping one changes the model.
Results are levels (.l) and marginals (.m); model and solver status must be checked after every solve.
Scaling, starting values and solver options (CONOPT, PATH, IPOPT) affect whether and where a solve converges.
MCP models pair equations with variables (=e= with complementarity); the pairing is part of the model.
Python targets: Pyomo or GAMSPy; Julia target: JuMP.

languages.name: GEMPACK (TABLO .tab, command .cmf; GTAP)
languages.run: tablo and the generated program, or rungtap; one .cmf per experiment
pitfalls: Equations are usually linearized percentage changes; a levels target (GAMS, Python) needs the levels form re-derived.
Solutions are multi-step (Euler or Gragg with extrapolation); the number of steps changes results for large shocks.
The closure (exogenous list) lives in the command file, not the model.
Data come from HAR files with headers; the GTAP database is licensed and never shared.
Equivalence with a levels model holds exactly only for small shocks; compare large shocks within the accuracy GEMPACK reports.

languages.name: AMPL
pitfalls: .mod is shared with Dynare; the inventory tells them apart by content.
Model, data and run files are separate and must be translated together.

languages.name: Fortran (77 and 90+)
pitfalls: Without IMPLICIT NONE, names starting with I to N are integers and others are single precision.
REAL is 32-bit; the literal 0.1 is single precision even when assigned to DOUBLE PRECISION (use 0.1d0).
Arrays are column-major and start at 1 unless other bounds are declared.
Integer division truncates (3/2 is 1).
COMMON blocks, EQUIVALENCE and SAVE create shared and persistent state.
Arguments are passed by reference, so a routine can change its caller's variables, including aliased ones.
Fixed form (Fortran 77): column 1 marks comments, column 6 continuation, code ends at column 72.
GOTO and arithmetic IF need to be restructured, not copied.

languages.name: C and C++
pitfalls: Indexing starts at 0 and arrays are row-major.
Integer division truncates and float is 32-bit.
Undefined behavior (overflow, out-of-bounds access) can make results depend on compiler and flags.
Results can change with optimization flags (-ffast-math) and with the BLAS/LAPACK library linked.

languages.name: COBOL
languages.tests: compare output files record by record
pitfalls: Numbers are fixed-point decimals (PIC 9(7)V99); translate with exact decimal arithmetic (Python decimal, Java BigDecimal), never binary floating point.
Arithmetic truncates unless ROUNDED is given; intermediate precision follows compiler rules.
COMP-3 is packed decimal and signs may be overpunched in the last digit; record layouts come from copybooks (.cpy).
REDEFINES overlays several layouts on the same bytes; OCCURS DEPENDING ON gives variable-length tables.
Level-88 condition names are named tests on a field's value.
EBCDIC sorts letters and digits in a different order from ASCII, so sorted outputs differ after migration.
PERFORM THRU and GO TO define control flow by paragraph ranges; restructure carefully.
Files are fixed-width records; the record layout is the interface to everything else.

languages.name: Excel workbooks (formulas) and VBA macros
languages.run: open in Excel; macros run from the workbook
pitfalls: LOG is base 10 (LN is natural); ROUND rounds half away from zero, but VBA Round rounds half to even.
Date serial numbers start on 30 December 1899 in the 1900 system and treat 1900 as a leap year.
Iterative calculation (circular references) and Solver runs are part of the model; their settings must be recorded.
Hard-coded numbers inside formulas and hidden rows, columns or sheets carry assumptions.
Use python tools/intake.py formulas to list the formulas behind a calculation sheet before translating it.
Numbers have 15 significant digits; text that looks like numbers does not compute.

languages.name: Mathematica / Wolfram Language
pitfalls: Exact (symbolic, rational) arithmetic gives different numbers from floating point until N[] is applied.
Indexing starts at 1 with [[ ]]; .m is shared with MATLAB and Objective-C.
Symbolic derivations are best translated to SymPy (with symbolic-derivation-specialist), not to numeric code.

languages.name: Maple
pitfalls: Exact arithmetic until evalf; translate derivations to SymPy and numerics separately.

languages.name: Scilab
pitfalls: MATLAB-like syntax with different function names and defaults; 1-based and column-major.

languages.name: Stan, JAGS and BUGS (Bayesian models)
languages.run: cmdstan, rjags or the host language
languages.tests: posterior summaries with Monte Carlo error
pitfalls: BUGS and JAGS dnorm takes the precision (1/variance); Stan normal takes the standard deviation.
Truncation and censoring use different syntax (T(,) in JAGS, T[,] in Stan).
Samplers differ (Gibbs against Hamiltonian Monte Carlo); compare posterior summaries within Monte Carlo error, never draws.

languages.name: SQL
pitfalls: NULL uses three-valued logic: NULL = NULL is not true, and WHERE drops NULL comparisons.
Row order is not defined without ORDER BY.
Integer division truncates in some dialects; AVG and SUM ignore NULLs.
Dialects (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, SQLite) differ in functions and date handling.

general: Translate behavior, not syntax: write down what each piece of source code computes before writing target code.
Bugs in the source are preserved in the first translation and logged; they are fixed only after equivalence is shown, as a separate approved change.
Random draws do not reproduce across software even with the same seed; export the draws from the source run and read them in the target, or compare distributions.
Default options differ more often than functions do: standard errors, degrees of freedom, quantile definitions, filters, optimizer methods and tolerances.
Missing values, sorting, rounding, indexing and storage order are the most common causes of differences after translation.
A translation is complete only when the target reproduces the source outputs to stated tolerances, or the differences are explained.
